subject: exploding star
title: What If a Star Exploded Bright Enough to See at Noon? In 1054 One Did

scenes.text: What if a star exploded so bright you saw it at noon? In 1054 it happened.
On July 4th, 1054, Chinese astronomers logged a guest star in the constellation Taurus.
It outshone Venus. For 23 days it was visible in broad daylight, the third brightest thing in the sky after the Sun and Moon.
At night it hung there for nearly two years before fading away.
It was a star 6,500 light-years away blowing itself apart, its outer layers racing out at about a thousand miles a second.
Those layers are still flying today. We call them the Crab Nebula, ten light-years across, with a corpse at its heart spinning thirty times a second.

description:
What if a star exploded bright enough to see at noon? On 4 July 1054, Chinese astronomers recorded a guest star in Taurus that outshone Venus, stayed visible in daylight for 23 days and remained in the night sky for nearly two years.
It was a supernova about 6,500 light-years away. Its debris, still expanding at roughly a thousand miles a second, is the Crab Nebula, about ten light-years across, with a pulsar at its center spinning about 30 times a second.

first_comment: Rock art in the American Southwest may show the same event, a bright star next to a crescent moon. Which star would you want to see explode, from a safe distance, and what should we run through next?
